This allows us to describe the similarities and 
differences between sounds in a relatively 
precise and well-defined way:
/p/ and /b/ both have the same manner and 
place of articulation.
But /p/ and /b/ differ in the timing of 
phonation relative to the release of the closure 
(voicing).
This difference is analogous to the difference 
between /t/ and /d/. 
So we can talk in general about “the voiced 
stops” /b/, /d/, /g/, and so on, which is helpful 
for phonological descriptions.

text:
Consider how we established that I really 
do have two different low back vowels.
We had to find two different words in 
which the distinction between them 
depended on the difference between those 
vowels.
Minimal pairs are important for 
demonstrating contrast. 
If two phones are contrastive -- i.e., you 
can find a minimal pair where the 
difference between them results in a 
difference in meaning -- they are examples 
of different phonemes.

text:
Why do I keep insisting that phonemes are not letters?
It’s easy for literate people to imagine that speech is produced as an orderly stream of 
letter-like units. 
But it is nothing like that. 
Here’s a spectrogram of the sentence:  “A sore back is a real pain.”

text:
“The best analogy I have been able to think of for this is a very homely one.  Imagine 
a row of Easter eggs carried along a moving belt; the eggs are of various sizes, and 
variously colored, but not boiled.  At a certain point, the belt carries the row of eggs 
between the two rollers of a wringer, which quite effectively smash them and rub 
them more or less into each other. The flow of eggs before the wringer represents 
the series of impulses from the phoneme source; the mess that emerges from the 
wringer represents the output of the speech transmitter.  At a subsequent point, we 
have an inspector whose task it is to examine the passing mess and decide, on the 
basis of the broken and unbroken yolks, the variously spread-out albumen, and the 
variously colored bits of shell, the nature of the flow of eggs which previously 
arrived at the wringer. Note that he does not have to try to put the eggs together 
again—a manifest physical impossibility—but only to identify.     
The inspector represents the hearer.”
Hockett (1955)

text:
Derivational Morphology is a process that derives new words from existing 
“parts.”
The “parts” (or units) are called morphemes.
The word Morphology has a pretty transparent derivation, actually:
morph- (derived from the Greek? for “form”) 
+
-ology (also from Greek, here meaning something like “the study of”)
“the study of the forms of words.” 
Then a similar process gives you morpheme. We just learned about phonemes. 
“Phone” is another morpheme from the Greek (for “speech?”). 
What do we call a unit in text?
What is “graphology?”...oops.

text:
Derivational morphology is productive, but in limited ways
...also with respect to how widely and how regularly affixes are applied.
Consider:
stem + -hood -> a state of being, associated with the stem noun
brotherhood
sisterhood
knighthood (actually kind of odd, because two brothers share their brotherhood, but 
each knight has his own knighthood..)
*neighborhood -- perfectly good word, but -hood does a different job entirely
*friendhood  -- we say friendship instead, for, like, no apparent reason
*enemyhood -- maybe ought to be a word. I can only think of top-shelf items like 
“enmity” or “antagonism” for this concept...
(some examples from Liberman & Prince’s introductory Linguistics class at Penn: 
http://www.ling.upenn.edu/courses/Fall_1998/ling001/morphology2.html Liberman also blogs at 
http://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu)

Even zero derivation does complicated things with semantics.
Consider these strong associates of the noun “knife.” Are their 
meanings similar as verbs?
She can dish it out but she can’t take it.
He was born with a silver spoon and a forked tongue in his mouth.
They decided to table the issue after a day of inconclusive negotiations.
If you got really distracted by “silver spoon,” above, you may enjoy reading about Cognitive 
Linguistics, which we won’t talk about much in this class.

text:
More commonly, derivational morphology changes the 
pronunciation (and spelling) of a word, e.g., by adding 
affixes:
certificate /sər.ˈtI.fɨ.kɨt/
certification /ˌsər.tɨ.fɨ.ˈkeI.ʃən/
recertification /ˈri.sər.tɨ.fɨ.ˌkeI.ʃən/
Note how adding an affix can impact the phonology of the rest of the word. (This is 
one reason for “The Chaos” of English spelling, and why higher fidelity to the 
spoken form doesn’t necessarily improve readability. )
Also consider the noun and verb forms of:
record
invite           (“He did not receive an invite”/”We did not invite him”)
entrance      (not actually related to each other)
...where the major change is also stress.

text:
Inflectional morphology changes the meaning of words in a more predictable way:
PLURALS
knife(n) - knives 
one fork - two forks
one mouse - a lot of mice
3RD PERSON SINGULAR PRESENT
knife(v) - knifes 
I walk - she walks
you run - he runs
PAST
knife(v) - knifed
Today I walk - yesterday I walked
Today she sings - in the past, she sang
Menn puts this succinctly:
“...we’d think it was silly to have 
separate dictionary entries for the 
singular and plural forms of 
nouns.”
But note that the phonological 
process of inflecting words often 
has some irregularity to it. 
(This will be a big deal later when 
we talk about different language 
learning models, and kinds of 
developmental language 
impairment.)

text:
Inflectional morphology also depends on the syntax of the rest of the sentence.
In the phrase 
“two [noun]+pl” 
whatever noun goes there must be pluralized 
somehow. 
There are no syntactic processes like this for even very 
productive derivational forms. 
The closest I can think of is a formula, like:
“Once you [verb] it, you can un-[verb] it.” 
But that’s not exactly syntax.
(This will be important when we talk about models of 
speech production in the next few weeks.)
PLURALS
knife(n) - knives 
one fork - two forks
...etc.

Activation dynamics
Most models of this kind assume that 
activation unfolds over time.
One way to explain frequency effects is to 
assume that activation dynamics are tuned up 
by experience.
Every time you encounter a word, you might:
raise its baseline level of activation
strengthen incoming connections so it can be 
activated more quickly
change a threshold parameter...etc.
This is a very simple form of learning, of course.
.
Different computational models (like 
Rumelhart & McClelland’s 1986 Interactive 
Activation model shown here) simulate 
frequency effects in different ways

text:
In the 1870’s a number of German neurologists —
Lichtheim, Wernicke — began making more systematic 
observations of aphasia.
They ascribed specific losses of function to 
“disconnections” between “centers.”
So, a loss of the ability to understand spoken words 
might be due to a disconnection between “A” and “B.”
A loss of the ability to do verbatim repetition may be 
due to a disconnection between “A” and “M,” and so 
on.
This approach of describing “centers” for specific 
functions is an ancestor of a topic we’ll be dealing with 
later on in the course: “modularity”
Eling, P., & Whitaker, H. (2009). History of aphasia: 
from brain to language. In Handbook of clinical 
neurology (Vol. 95, pp. 571-582).

text:
Sigmund Freud (!) critiqued the “diagram-drawing” 
school of aphasia research in his early neurological 
research.
He felt it was naïve to expect the brain to be organized 
according to psychological categories like “word forms” 
or “concepts.”
He proposed instead that language emerged from 
“fields” connecting perceptual and motor abilities to 
“drives.” 
This is a durable tension in cognitive neuroscience:
Can we directly relate brain area functions and 
cognitive functions or not?
Is the brain really organized according to our 
descriptions of cognitive phenomena?
A holist critique

text:
Back to Leborgne’s brain...
Using MRI, Dronkers and colleagues were able 
to assess the extent and location of damage in 
Broca's landmark cases very precisely.
The lesion is very deep, and includes the insula. 
There is also a lot of white matter damage to 
the superior longitudinal fasciculus (which, 
basically connects the front and back of the 
cerebral cortex).
Indeed, other work by this group suggests that 
the insula, not Broca's area, is strongly 
associated with speech apraxia (the condition 
Broca described in his patients).

text:
The Functional Level -- Lemmas
No, not Lemmings.
(The term “lemma” is 
borrowed from mathematics, 
where it refers to a 
proposition in an argument.)
And they do not just follow 
each other blindly off cliffs, 
BTW.
We can’t just say that we select the “words” that 
we’re going to produce at the functional level… 
Why not?
Consider this error:
Where’d I put it when I brought it in  Where’d I 
bring it when I put it in.
So, the verbs switched places, but the actual words 
that were produced reflect a change in tense that 
must have been applied later. 
This couldn’t have happened if the word “brought” 
was selected. Rather, we say the lemma BRING was 
selected, and was expressed as present tense…

The Functional Level
Why do people so often say the opposite of what they mean?
Antonyms are actually quite similar at a number of levels:
 
- semantically related
 
- strongly associated 
 
… it’s like a perfect storm in the spreading activation framework… 
 
further:
 
- can take on the same semantic roles
 
- same word class (can take on same syntactic roles)
 
...so the rest of the speech production system can handle them…
So it’s easy for activation to spread from a lemma to its antonym.

text:
The Functional Level
Functional (Semantic) roles. 
Remember:
{The plums} {in the icebox} were eaten {by me}
{Undergoer} + {Location} + Verb + {Agent}
Alternatively:
I + have eaten {the plums} {in the icebox}.
Agent + Verb + Undergoer + Location
So, we have a simple event structure, and we can start slotting 
lemmas into semantic roles. We know that the Verb will be TO EAT, 
the Agent of the verb will be ME, and that PLUM will be the 
Undergoer, etc.
Note there are syntactic consequences for arranging these roles in 
different orders, with consequences for how we turn the lemma for 
ME into a word. 
That will happen at the Positional Level, in our next session…

text:
The Positional Level
Let’s take the simple-seeming sentence we used as evidence that lemmas are a useful concept:
 
Where’d I bring it when I put it in?
By the time we’re done at the functional level, we know: 
 
1. that we have two Verbs PUT and BRING
 
2. that I/ME is the Agent of both verbs
 
3. that IT is the Undergoer of both verbs
What else? 
What is the temporal relationship between the verbs?
Expressing all of those things syntactically is what goes on at the Positional Level.

text:
If we skip the part where we organize the sentence into a question, and work out the 
appropriate tenses for the verbs, etc., we get something like:
 
Where’d I [verb, root form] it when I [verb, past] it in?
(Actually, rather a lot of syntactic work had to happen to get that first clause right, 
because we have both Wh- movement and an auxiliary verb to form the question.) 
What we are paying attention to here is that that structure of the first clause requires the 
base form of the lemma in English.
…and then the next clause requires the past form.
So, what we have at the Positional Level is a syntactic structure with slots for all of the 
lemmas we activated at the Functional Level, along with all of the other particles 
required by the grammar.
An error like “Where’d I bring it when I put it in,” can be thought of as arising while the 
slots generated by the Positional Level are being filled with lemmas activated at the 
Functional level.

Oldfield and Wingfield eventually addressed this by matching 
their high- and low-frequency words for length.
They found a robust frequency effect, so they concluded that

an attempt to demonstrate that some observed effect is not just 
an effect of some other confounding variable…

text:
Belke et al.
In speech production, we have to distinguish carefully between activation and selection.
Spreading activation from, e.g., duck to fish means that activating one can help activate 
the other. But this can cause problems when our task is to select the correct lemma from a 
bunch of active ones…
The WEAVER++ model assumes that selection time is determined by a ratio of the activity 
of the most active lemma and the overall activation of all lemmas.
Thus, when there’s feedback from the category level, this slows down lemma selection 
because of all the collateral activation for items from the same category.
